rv.q: What makes Staunton so good in the title role is her ability to tease with her treasurableness: she coats steely exploitation with jaunty allure; the revelation of her sheer calculation produces a shudder.
Cooke’s pared-back production lets that modernity shine out, scrapping all that tedious late-Victorian stage business of tablecloths and rattling teacups in favour of a simple circle of greenery...

Carter’s Vivie is the centre of the play, and Carter imbues this unconventional woman with the appropriate mix of modern and traditional sensibilities … Staunton is too smart, too empathetic an actor to aim to overpower her fellow actors.

Staunton and Carter make a wonderful double act, bringing painful emotional truth to the twisting narrative, as Shaw attacks, with robust vigour and diagrammatic clarity, the hypocrisy and inequality of late Victorian society.

A bit stagey, perhaps, but Dominic Cooke’s period revival brings into partial view the vast cattle market Shaw so impolitely exposed, ensuring his play was banned (by men, of course) for almost three decades.
Topical in a way – what hidden agonies fund well-heeled or Western lifestyles today? – but elsewhere a tepidity sets in.
The play flares fully to life in their duologues but the scenes around them feel filled with extraneous, thinly drawn characters and plot.
This latest outing doesn’t quite manage to complete a hat-trick of undisputed triumphs, but it is never less than a fascinating evening’s theatre.
But if you're hoping for something closer to the bone, you may find this a little too professional.
The symbolism is heavy-handed and aside from Robert Glenister’s leering businessman Sir George Crofts, the men in Kitty and Vivie’s orbit never really seem more than a neatly ordered set of opinions.
There’s an inescapable sense, though, of artificiality; the ideas neatly stacked up, but the humanity oddly absent.

Cooke’s slimline text and his lavish production turn a remarkably punchy 130-year old play into exactly what you fear an evening of Bernard Shaw might be: worthy and dull, plonked in the West End because it’s a too-tempting vehicle for an acting legend and a Bridgerton star.
Cooke's swift touch direction gently dials up the heat with the gentleness of a paintbrush, but with the momentum of punch to the stomach.
The result is an extraordinary tour de force that brings the play to vivid and compelling life.

Carter is outstanding as the robustly pragmatic Vivie, whose assured sense of self is shattered by a series of revelations, including about her mother’s work, her elusive father, and various circling suitors.
Cooke has shortened a long play to well below two hours, played without interval, and his production proceeds at a smart pace with consistent performances from the whole cast.
The production is utterly conventional without ever being dull.
The result is always keen-eyed and fascinating, as one has long come to expect from Cooke...

Perhaps the plan was to add layers of emotional depth to the story but the experiment doesn’t work because the Vivie-Kitty relationship is based on distance and alienation, not on love and propinquity.
Truly timeless, it cascades from revelation to revelation like a concerto, never seemingly to favour one character nor viewpoint.
Imelda Staunton and real-life daughter Bessie Carter go toe-to-toe in this polished, throaty version of George Bernard Shaw's Mrs Warren's Profession...

Cooke does his best with this dated setup where women are deemed little more than marriage material but, even with a few inspired nips and tucks here and there, this production sags and drags in places.
Staunton’s command of the stage is magnetic—her every glance and gesture loaded with the weight of a woman who has clawed her way to security in a world that offered her none.
In Cooke’s hands, it still goes off with a bang.
But the exercise nevertheless comes off as oddly dry.

cn.t: Shaw's 1893 play gets a lean, brisk revival elevated by powerhouse real-life mother-daughter duo Staunton and Carter, whose compelling performances spark genuine electricity. Critics are divided on whether the trimmed text feels fresh or remains too verbose and didactic.

vr.q: The production feels in some ways a little at odds with itself. There's still much to enjoy about it.
